utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. President. Case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to greet everyone in the courtroom, members of the Prosecution, Defence counsel, the accused, and everyone else in the courtroom. First there are four oral decisions I have to render concerning the admissibility of documents. The first one concerns a document that relates to Witness BP. The Trial Chamber will declare its position concerning the admission into evidence of a document relating to Witness BP who appeared on the 4th and 5th of October, 2006. The Trial Chamber decides to admit into evidence the following exhibits presented by the Prosecution because they have probative value and relevance: P 09715 under seal, P 04161 under seal. In addition, the Trial Chamber notes that the Defence hasn't requested that any documents be admitted into evidence. On the other hand, the Trial Chamber would like to point out that it has decided not to admit the following documents presented by the Prosecution since they don't appear authentic, relevant, and they don't seem to have sufficient probative value: P 03855 is concerned. And now for my second -- for our second oral decision, the corrigendum. On the 5th of October, 2006, the Chamber rendered an oral decision concerning the admission into evidence of documents that related to Witness BQ. As far as document P 04588 is concerned, the Trial Chamber would like to note that only the photographs shown to the witness will be admitted. This concerns the four photographs with the following numbers: 0361/7095 -- 7095. And could we have a slash between the 1 and 7. The second photograph is 0361-7106. There's a hyphen, not a slash. Next photograph is 0361-7111. That's correct. And finally 0361-7152. And now for the third oral decision that concerns the admission into evidence of documents relating to Witness BO. The Trial Chamber will rule on the admission into evidence today on documents that concern Witness BO, who appeared on the 4th of October, 2006. The Trial Chamber admits into evidence the following documents presented by the Prosecution, given that they have a certain probative value and relevance. I will now list the documents: P 09717 under seal, P 09309, P 03480, P 03498, P 04161, P 04177, P 09265, P 04432, P 04605, P 04836. In addition, the Chamber will admit the following documents presented by the Defence, since they have a certain probative value and a certain relevance: 3D 00829 -- 429.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction. 3D 00429.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] IC 00044. There are three 0's. IC 00044. On the other hand, the Trial Chamber won't admit the following documents into evidence presented by the Prosecution because Witness BO could not shed light on the authenticity, relevance, or probative value on these documents. These documents are P 04203, P 04203 and P 07134. And now for the fourth oral decision and the last one, an oral decision concerning the admission into evidence of the documents relating to the testimony of Witness Ibrahim Sahic. P 08534 is the document concerned. On the 27th of September, 2006, the Prosecution submitted a written motion to the Chamber requesting the admission into evidence of a new copy of the document with the provisional number P 08534. In this case a death certificate was concerned concerning Adem Adibovic [as interpreted], who -- which was presented to the witness Ibrahim Sahic when he appeared on the 17th of October -- on the 17th of August, 2006. The Prosecution stated that following the objections made by Mr. Kovacic that concerned the illegibility of the names and dates in the copy of the document it had requested and obtained a new copy of this document which was legible, entirely legible. The Chamber would like to point out that on the 24th of August, 2006, it orally decided to mark P 08534 for identification while waiting for the Prosecution to provide a better copy. On the 28th of September, 2006, Mr. Kovacic filed a reply to the Prosecution's motion opposing the admission into evidence of this document, claiming that pursuant to Rule 89(D), the probative value of this document was significantly inferior to the need for a fair trial, given that the date of death on the death certificate was two days earlier than the date of death mentioned by the witness. On the other hand, the witness only identified the surname of the person who died and said that this was a very common surname. The Trial Chamber would like to remind you that pursuant to the decision of the 13th of July, 2006, that concerns the admission into evidence of documents and in conformity with the jurisprudence of this Tribunal evidence must have a certain amount of relevance and a certain probative value if it is to be admitted. The Chamber reserves the right to render a definitive decision about the weight to be attached to a document at the end of the presentation of evidence, of all evidence. In this case, the Chamber notes that the new copy of the death certificate provided by the Prosecution has sufficient indicia of reliability given that the death certificate -- to the extent that the death certificate of Adem Adibovic -- Hebibovic, H-e-b-o-v-i-c. I'll repeat the name because there's a mistake again. Hebibovic, H-e-b-i-b-o-v-i-c. This was shown to the witness Ibrahim Saric and also has sufficient indicia of probative value and reliability. The Chamber decides to admit into evidence document P 08534. The Trial Chamber, however, takes into account the objections raised by Mr. Kovacic, and when determining the weight to be attached to this document in the light of all the evidence presented to the Chamber. That's the fourth decision. I thought that Mr. Murphy had something to say, wanted to take the floor. If you want to take up a few minutes, you may take the floor, Mr. Murphy. Otherwise, you should do so later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. I hope that my voice will last. I'm suffering from a cold, but I will do my best to be understood. Your Honour, my purpose in taking the floor is essentially to advise the Trial Chamber on behalf of all the accused and their counsel of a motion that we will be filing later today and also to make an oral application for leave to exceed the word limit in respect of this motion. The only reason that I mention it today is that it's a motion which is somewhat unusual, indeed, we believe may be unparalleled in the history of this Tribunal, and I want to give the Trial Chamber in just about two minutes an overview of the motion and why we regard it as a very serious matter. Your Honours know that there have been two -- at least two subsidiary proceedings in this case of that have been the subject of some litigation. The first was -- Are we in private session, Your Honour? I'm sorry. May we go into private session for a short time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The testimony of Witness BR is commencing in open session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You just told us that in 1992 you were living in Prozor. Until when did you live in Prozor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until the end of August 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to take you back to September of 1992. Could you describe to the Court the situation between the Bosnian Muslims and the Bosnian Croats in the town of Prozor at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Relations at that time between the Bosnian Croats and Muslims were tense. Incidents erupted. In the Bosniak houses, they were destroyed. But anyway, the situation was tense.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you talk about incidents that erupted could you be more specific and give one example of an incident that you are aware of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For instance, here is an example: When the HVO soldiers bashed on the windows and -- of Muslim houses, for example.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did the situation evolve in the next month; that is, October of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In October 1992, relations came to a head. They worsened so that on the 23rd of October, an armed conflict broke out between the BH army and the Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before going into more details about the 23rd of October, would I like to show you document number 00680 [sic]. There is a bundle just next to you, and you will see that there is a tab marked 608. That is the document I am referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may make a general objection at this point in time. Yesterday Mr. Scott stood up with respect to yesterday's witness and said that the gentleman should not be commenting on any documents which he was unaware of at the time, and so I took a special note of that, because I see that all of the documents virtually are from sources which obviously this witness would not have been aware of. So I would like to know now is the Prosecution reversing that position? Are they maintaining that position? Because what's good for the goose is also good for -- as we know what.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It's not the same at all in fact. What the Prosecution has understood from the Chamber's prior rulings and the distinction is the difference between a witness that talk about either the authenticity of the document or the content of the document. On a number of occasions yesterday Mr. Kljuic was shown documents in which he could do neither. He knew nothing about the document. It wasn't his document, nor did he know anything about the substance of the document. But nonetheless, we spent a great deal of the afternoon reading documents and then having the question, Did I read that correctly; yes, you read it correctly. Those are the words on the written page. But have no knowledge of either the content or the authenticity. This witness and granted absolutely transparent on our case may not -- may not be her documents but they are the documents, the content of which she can address. If she can't, then we'll be corrected and the Chamber will not admit the exhibits. There's not -- it's not the same thing at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. So we're talking about the contents of a document. Now, with respect to content, Ms. Egels.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness BR, can I ask you to read the content of the document numbered 608. It's a very short content.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: And if Your Honour wishes, she might read it out loud, if it might be easier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again -- excuse me, madam. If we look at this document, and I certainly don't want to be, you know, obstreperous, but if we look at the document and we look and see what the document contains, I don't see how, keeping with the Prosecutor's last comment or their response to my objection, how we can conduct a hearing in this fashion. I mean, it's one thing to take a narrative from the witness what happened in Prozor, please describe to us. Now we're going into documents asking her to speculate as to whether something in the document may be accurate. I don't see how this is -- I've never experienced, you know, this sort of an examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is not where the problem lies, Mr. Karnavas. The witness said that the situation had deteriorated as time went by, and we're talking about the 23rd of October, 1992. She said that the situation had deteriorated, and here we have a document where the first sentence states precisely that. "The situation in town deteriorated," or, "is deteriorating." So to ask whether this document coincides with what she thinks and what she saw, that's another matter, but the second paragraph relates to an incident. Now, in order to gain time we're going to the heart of the matter straight away; otherwise, we're going to lose a lot of time. Perhaps the Defence wishes to waste time. But instead of saying -- we said -- the Prosecutor could have asked, "Could you give us some incidents," and she might have mentioned the incident of the flag. But let's try not to waste time and without prejudicing your client. So we have wasted quite a number of minutes now, and it doesn't serve any purpose, Mr. Karnavas. As Judge Trechsel said, you are not before an American Tribunal. You're in an international Tribunal which uses the mixed system. And I'd like to remind you of focusing, for example on the Nuremberg trial, and you will have seen that the Nuremberg trial, which was the first time that international justice held a case of that kind, there were thousands of documents that were admitted in written form. Now, here we have a document relating to an incident concerning a flag, which appeared on the police building. So that's the heart of the matter, the basic premise. Now, if the Prosecution wishes to raise this type of issue and if you keep objecting, we'll be here for years and years.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't mean to be objecting, but let's -- let's look at it objectively speaking. And I'm very familiar with the Nuremberg approach and I have no objections to that. After the hoisting of the Croatian flag. Have we heard any time from this particular witness about the hoisting of a flag? The answer is no. That is a fact not in evidence from this particular witness. It's called leading. Secondly, it goes on to say, there is a possibility that a large-scale clash will occur in the town. Again, how can this witness comment? She can be asked what happened in Prozor on these days, and she can tell us a flag was hoisted and what happened next? Well, there were clashes. That's the way to approach it. But now to bring in these documents through the back door, I don't see the purpose. I'll sit down. I won't make any objection. But frankly, I don't think this is way to take evidence. That's my professional opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Egels.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Going back to the first sentence of this document, Witness BR: "The situation in town is deteriorating," just as you told us a few minutes ago. This is a document dated the 20th of October of 1992. Do you remember the incident of the flag on this police building?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Leading.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I remember this document well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You remember this document or you remember the incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember the incident.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you explain what you saw concerning this incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw a flag flying on the police station, and immediately after that the people working in the MUP, the Muslims working in MUP, were sacked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say you remember a flag flying on the police station, could you be more specific? What flag was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the Croatian flag with the chequer-board emblem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You just told us that the situation erupted on the 23rd of October of 1992. Could you tell the Court what happened on the 23rd of October, 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On that day there were negotiations between the Croatian Defence Council and the Territorial Defence on the security situation in the municipality. However, at those negotiations it was agreed that there would be no conflict. But the army, the soldiers who were already in town, many soldiers came into town and they were told to go to Jajce, to defend Jajce because Jajce was in danger. However, at about 3.00 p.m. or 3.30 p.m. shooting started in town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You just said that there were negotiations between the Croatian Defence Council and the Territorial Defence. How are you aware of these negotiations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since I worked in the municipality at the time, the president who sat in the municipality together with us left to attend the negotiations, and they said there were negotiations being conducted between the Territorial Defence and the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you give us the name of the president of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The president of the municipality was named Misko Jusic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know any other person attending these negotiations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I knew Nikola Ivic. He attended the negotiations too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was Nikola Ivic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was of the president of the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The president of the Executive Board of what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any other persons present at these negotiations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. On the Bosniak side there was Muharem Sabic, the commander of the Territorial Defence; and then there was Esad Bektas, secretary of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You then told us that around 3.00 p.m. the shooting started. Do you know why the shooting started? Are you aware of the reasons or what started this fighting, this shooting? Were you still present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So do you know why the violence erupted, why the shooting started?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At 3.00 -- in the afternoon of the 23rd, Witness BR, where were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was at home in my house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did the shooting start? Did you hear it? Did you see it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It started in town and in the surrounding villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any shooting in your neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did happen to your neighbourhood on the 23rd of October of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 23rd of October, 1992, well, the armed conflict broke out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But what about your neighbourhood? What happened to you? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ah, to me. I was at home with my mother, and we heard the shooting. The shooting lasted throughout the night. However, on the 24th, in the morning hours, the house was burnt. Our house was burnt. The HVO burnt my house, the house I was in with my mother.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you give us some more details and walk us through the events of the 24th when your house was burnt. How did it start?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is how it was: The HVO soldiers came up to the front door. They bashed in the door, stormed into the house and set fire to the house, and we were still in the house on the ground floor, and they did all this on the upper floor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know these were HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I know because they wore chequer-board insignia. And I personally recognised one of my neighbours who was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Maybe if we could go to private session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So do you recognise the place, the location on this picture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court what location this is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is Kucani.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are we talking about Exhibit 9704?

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Just for the record, Your Honours, I believe the witness was looking at another exhibit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So are we now looking at Exhibit 9704, Witness BR?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise this location?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us where this is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Podgradje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this where you stayed during the month of August 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since we have the photo in front of us, madam, to the right we can see there's a space with a construction covered by a plastic sheet, and there are these little blocks on it. What was there? What was that, as far as you can remember?

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, but again I think we are not talking about the same picture. I see that the one that is displayed is 9705 and not 04. It seems there is a mix between two pictures.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The photograph we have on the screen is 9704; is that correct? Madam, can you see the photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can see to the right there is a construction covered in a plastic sheet with blocks on top of it. What was there before, a house, in 1993? Can you remember what there was there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Ms. Egels, please continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness BR, how do you know this is Podgradje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I know because I stayed there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise any -- any feature on this picture that would help you recognise Podgradje and not another part of town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can recognise all these houses and the owners, and I'm certain that this is Podgradje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that you left Podgradje at the end of August 1993, that you were expelled, and that you arrived in Bugojno. I would like you now --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- to turn to a little bit later in time, in 1994. What were you doing? What was your job at that time in the beginning of 1994?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In 1994, I worked in Bugojno municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at one point in time in 1994 did you work for the state commission for gathering facts on war crimes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That was from March to August 1994.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was your job at this commission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I took statements from women, from the victims of abuse, in the commission. So that's what my job consisted of on the whole.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Your Honour, maybe if we could return to private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Ms. Egels, does that complete your examination-in-chief then?

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I just would like to ask you to tender into evidence the exhibits that I've shown to the witness. Number P 00608, P 00673 under seal, P 00679, P 02999, P 03234, P 09704, and two other exhibits that have already been admitted, but I would ask the Court to put them under seal, P 00640 and P 09376. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could the registrar tell me how much the Prosecution used -- how much time the Prosecution used so that we can give the same amount of time to the Defence. While that is being done, I'm going to -- well, the registrar has just informed me that the Prosecution used 70 minutes, which means one hour and 10 minutes. I turn to the Defence, and who is going to start off? Counsel Nozica.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I apologise, but can you tell me how much time I have? The Prosecution took 70 minutes. So how much time do I have, 10 minutes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if it's 70 divided by 6, that gives you about 10 minutes each.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I was thinking about the cross-examination, so I wasn't doing the calculations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But in 10 minutes you can ask a lot of questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed. Thank you. To start off, can we go back into private session, because I have a personal question to ask?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're back in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the beginning of your testimony, you said that you worked in the municipality. You gave us quite a lot of details. You knew a lot of things. Can you remember or do you have any knowledge of where the TO members in 1992, until October, as you said, together with members of the HVO were? Where were they together? At what positions and who was on the other side, on the opposite side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not quite clear about your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While they were together, the HVO members and TO members, did they hold any positions vis-a-vis the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did hold positions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where? Where? What positions? Where was that? In the town of Prozor, around Prozor, where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the surrounding parts around Prozor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know exactly where but I know they held positions together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Around Prozor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they hold any positions facing Kupres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they hold joint positions, for example, at Crni Vrh?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember about Crni Vrh, but I know that they did for Kupres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether the TO members dug any trenches or held any positions at Crni Vrh itself, Makljen, towards Makljen, up at Crni Vrh, mount Crni Vrh?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't know. Right. Now, in your statement you said -- I'm going to slow down. The Court hasn't reprimanded me yet, so I'll do so myself. We speak the same language, so let's make pauses between question and answer. When you spoke about organised torching of houses, can you tell me, please, or, rather, repeat already -- you've already said that. Who was Ivan Dole? Did you say he was an HVO member?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember that you in fact gave a statement to the OTP on the 6th of February, 2002, in which you describe these events?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll remind you just part -- a part of your statement where you say on page 5: "In front of the house, on the path I mentioned between the torched house of my father and my uncle, (redacted), I saw Ivo Dole. Together with him we fled to the nearby woods."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, strike the name Ismet, please, from the record.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So "together with him we fled to the nearby woods in order to hide from HVO soldiers." Is that correct, is that what you've said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me tell you, madam, to the nearby house, because the road to Ivo's house led through the woods.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why were you hiding with an HVO member, Ivo Dole, from other members of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we were afraid. Imagine a situation in which you were a house -- in a house which had already been half burnt to the ground. It's terrible fear, and you had to hide. You hide from yourself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about your fear. That's quite normal and understandable. I'm asking you why Ivo Dole hid with you from the other members of the HVO. Did he know them? Did he say he knew them? Did he say he knew what they were doing there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was like this, madam: He wasn't in hiding nor were we in hiding. That path led to his house. The path through the woods led to his house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what you say here is not in fact correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe it was wrongly presented and stated wrongly, because the path led through the woods to his house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let me ask you it this way: Did he go with you, Ivo Dole?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he was with you; he didn't stay with the other HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. He went with us, together with us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you talk to him about who these other soldiers were and what they were doing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't talk to him? You didn't ask him who are those men, what are they doing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't ask him anything, because at that point in time -- no, I didn't ask him anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you with him for a time at his place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For how long?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Five days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During those five days did you ever ask who those people were? Did he know those people? Did he know why they were doing what they were doing, on whose orders? Did you ask him any of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we asked him none of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we now have on e-court document 00679. It's a document presented to the witness, and it is in fact a document from the head of the Main Staff of the HVO, General Milivoj Petkovic. It is dated the 31st of October.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you see underneath the date here, I'm referring to the Croatian version, that it says: "To prevent the unruly behaviour of individuals."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in view of the situation and the situation that you described, that a member of the HVO was hiding you in his house, that you saw some people who were doing things like that, do you stand by the assertion or conviction that the torching of houses during that period of time was organised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I still claim that, that it was organised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you ought to know that the BH army or, rather, the defence ministry for each individual leaving the municipality would have to issue a permit for them to do so; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Bugojno municipality and the department for national defence in the municipality at the time you were working there, did it have to issue for all military conscripts or anybody who had to do military service be issued with a permit if they wanted to leave the municipality? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the situation is exactly the same as you described it in Prozor when the HVO issued permits. Would that be the same situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you this. I worked in Bugojno when there was no conflict. The conflict had already ceased in Bugojno when I arrived there in 1994 and worked in Bugojno. There wasn't a conflict going on there anymore.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, you have the education you told us you have. I can't repeat what it is in open session, but was it a war situation? Was there the imminent threat of war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were the same provisions and regulations applied during a war and during imminent war? You were in Bugojno during the war situation. It doesn't matter that there were no conflicts going on at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So did the same permits have to be issued throughout the territory where a situation of war existed regardless of the fact of which authorities controlled the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that in Bugojno permits were issued to people who wished to leave the municipality, so that anybody wishing to leave would be issued a permit if he wasn't a military recruit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened to military recruits if they asked for permits to leave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They didn't -- they weren't issued with permits.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about those who had a work assignment like you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They weren't issued permits either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they could request a permit but weren't issued with a permit; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the meantime -- and I thank my colleagues, I have been given Mr. Ibrisimovic's time. I'll just use a bit of it. May we have a look at the next permit - it is Exhibit number 2999, which was shown to the witness - for some so clarification. Madam, would you take a look at this, please. It is an order, in fact. And when we read the order, we can see that they regulate relations on this territory because it says: "I emphasise once again that passes issued by other civilian and military organs in the municipality should not be recognised and that these persons should be returned." So do we agree that this order, and you've read it -- well, during preparations for your testimony did you see this order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we agree, you and I, that this order in fact regulates relations on a given territory and states who can issue passes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you agree with me that in Bugojno municipality, that is to say where you were, that these rules applied as well, that it was only the Secretariat for National Defence who was able and permitted to issue passes of this kind or permits of this kind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I wanted to focus on one particular point, and it is this. The sentence which says: "This order shall apply to persons of Muslim ethnicity as well." "To persons of Muslim ethnicity as well." There's a problem. It says this order -- not that one. "Also applied to persons of Muslim ethnicity." That's what it says in the document. Does that mean logically to you and me that it refers to everybody else, to the Croats, to the Serbs, and to persons of Muslim ethnicity? Am I right in stating that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, just briefly, something about your work in this commission. Can you tell the Court, please -- can you give the full name of the commission to the Court? What was it called?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The commission for investigating war crimes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who headed the commission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mirza Pogarca [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mirsad Tokaca was the name. Tokaca Mirsad; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm just looking at the transcript to get the name right. Do you agree with me that the commission was actually called the state commission for gathering information on war crimes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I just gave you the abridged version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. But it was a state commission.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, a state commission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, while -- you were working as a volunteer; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were working as a volunteer for that commission, did you have any knowledge of, did you have an assignment to or knew about anybody collecting information about crimes committed in Bugojno against Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't work on that yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't have an assignment of that kind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't know that anybody in the commission gathered information of that kind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You as a citizen of Bugojno, did you hear that there were crimes committed against Croats and that Croats were in prisons, too, that they were killed, that their wives were raped and so on, women were raped and so on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear about that. I didn't wish to hear anything about that. I had enough problems of my own from my own people, and I didn't talk to anybody about things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you said, "I had enough of my own," what do you mean your own?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had my own problems. That's what I meant. Problems of my own. So when you have your own problems you don't have time to deal with other people's.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you did deal with other people's problems. You listened to women, heard their statements, Bosniak women who were raped by Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So those are your problems. You considered those to be your problems; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, it's like this. They were the problems in my own municipality. I'm sure that somebody worked for the Bugojno municipality to collect information of that kind. I didn't know what they did, just as they didn't know what I did for the Prozor municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your work did you ever receive any information according to which some Croats were abused, arrested, expelled, that their houses were torched, that they were killed, anything like that? During that period of time, because you occupied a very important post. Lots of people went through your office. I assume everybody, the whole town goes through your offices. So everybody had problems to solve and go to the office that you worked in, not to mention your exact work post. Did you ever hear of things like that happening to Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't work in Bugojno for a long time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But during that brief period of time did you hear about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, whoever had a problem asked for Mr. Vlaco [as interpreted] and spoke to him. I really don't know how or why they came.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anyone speak to you out of the individuals that you contacted about war crimes? Did they tell you about crimes against Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they spoke about crimes, but I couldn't say anything about that. I didn't see them. I wasn't there during the conflict.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told the Chamber, with regard to the rape of Muslim women and their names, you said that you found out about these crimes because someone told you about them. You followed the line of information. Did you do the same to find out what had happened to Croats if you heard that something had happened to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had no authority to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the next Defence team, please. Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours. My colleague, Ms. Nozica, says that we should correct something in the transcript. On page 72, line 18, it should say Mlaco, with an M, instead of Vlaco. So the first letter is wrong.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, good day. My name is Vesna Alaburic. I'm a lawyer from Zagreb, and I represent General Milivoj Petkovic in these proceedings. I have a few questions for you that concern your testimony, and that also concern the written statements you provided to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not from the security service in Bugojno, in Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I apologise. In Prozor. You said that you handed over the statements to him; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether while gathering those statements, while taking those statements you cooperated with him by asking him for any explanations, assistance to locate women, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I did this myself. I performed such duties myself. I looked for the women and took statements from them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So can we conclude that when taking statements from raped women you cooperated exclusively with the security service and not with the state commission for investigating war crimes?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. But I'm interested in your direct link.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, I'm interested in your communication with this individual. According to your testimony, while gathering or taking statements, you didn't cooperate with anyone in the state commission for investigating war crimes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I have just told you how I did this.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that this was through the security service. But you did not have direct contact with the state commission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, with regard to the statements that you took, did you ever testify about these statements before a court, or did you contribute to the institution of proceedings in any other way and to the sanctions being taken against the perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that the women you interviewed told you how they had been raped by HVO soldiers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Are you sure that the women you interviewed said that exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Some of the women you have interviewed have testified here, and their testimony doesn't correspond to what you have said. They said that there were men who arrived in civilian clothing. They also mentioned members of other units, and this is why I'm now asking you. On what basis did the women you interviewed come to the conclusion that the men involved were HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they came to that conclusion because the men who were in uniforms with the chequer-boards and they knew they were HVO soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So you are sure that the all the women that you interviewed said that those who had raped them were HVO soldiers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, according to their statements, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: According to their statements.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I know what the women said when they gave me their statements. I can't write anything else down.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm just trying to ask you whether you are quite sure that those were the contents of their statements.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes. The statements I took reflected what they said. I noted down what they actually said.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: As far as the investigating war crimes are concerned - I only have another two questions - according to your information to the state commission for investigating war crimes had the task of investigating all crimes committed in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes, it did have that task.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you have any information according to which that state commission determined that -- that a crime was committed by the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I assume they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, did the state commission for investigating war crimes publish the results of its investigations in books and reviews about crimes committed in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Is there a lot of literature about the subject, unfortunately a lot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And in all these publications published by the state commission for war crimes, did you ever come across information on crimes committed by members of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In which publication? Which crime is in question? Could you tell us, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, for example, crimes committed in Uzdol, Gabravica, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And these publications were published by the state commission for war crimes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've heard about those war crimes, but believe me, right now I cannot remember everything.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: On the basis of your answer can we draw the conclusion that you cannot claim for certain that you ever found out that the state commission for war crimes published information on war crimes committed by members of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really couldn't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I now have some questions that concern the incident with the flag in Prozor on the 20th of October, 1992. In response to a question from the Prosecution, you said that on the 20th of October, 1992, a chequer-board flag was flown from the police building, a Croatian flag.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When this flag was hoisted, was some other flag taken down from that building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know, believe me. I'm not aware of any other flag being there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And next to the Croatian flag was there some other flag?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And a day earlier, on the 19th of October, on the police building could you tell us whether there was a flag on the police building then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Would you pass by the police building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: How is it that you saw -- or, rather, did you see the Croatian flag on the police building on the 20th of October?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 20th of October I was told that there was a Croatian flag that had been hoisted, and then I later passed by and saw it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: How did you hear about the Croatian flag flying from the building, and why was this new? Why should people speak about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't particularly important because at the time I worked in Prozor municipality and, well, they said there was a Croatian flag on the -- flying from the police station. And then I passed by and saw it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Like my colleague, Nozica, I would like to refer your to your educational background and your knowledge of the judicial system in Bosnia-Herzegovina. My question is as follows: As a rule, buildings that were part of a state body, that belonged to a state body, did they usually have flags flying from them? The municipality building, for example, the police building, the state inspector's office, tax office, et cetera, did these buildings have flags flying from them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes. So it would be logical for there to be a flag flying from the police station before the 20th of October?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you whether that would be logical.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it would be logical to expect there to be a flag there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Would you be surprised if I told you that on the 20th of October, 1992, both the Croatian flag and the flag of Bosnia and Herzegovina were flying from that building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You said that hoisting the Croatian flag provoked a Muslim revolt to a certain extent.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to us what the flag of Bosnia and Herzegovina looked like at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The flag of Bosnia and Herzegovina had lilies on it at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: It had lilies on it. Thank you. You also said that on the 20th of October, 1992, the Muslim police members were dismissed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you see any letter of dismissal that had been provided to Muslim policemen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean in a written letter?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't see any written letters, but I know that these people didn't go to work.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: They didn't go to work. I'm interested in that. Why did you come to the conclusion that these individuals didn't go to work, because they had been fired?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they were not allowed to enter the building.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Well, according to the information you had, who prevented them from entering the building? Who forbade it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: How -- what's your source of information, according to which they were not allowed to enter the building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what the reason was.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you know that because the Croatian flag had been hoisted on the police building the Muslims -- the Muslim policemen were so revolted they decided not to go to work? Were you provided with such information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I'm not familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I now have a number of questions that concern the houses that were set on fire. Please have a look at P 09376. Could we have the document on the screen too. It's a document that we have already seen. It's a description of the houses that were set on fire. Witness, we can now see the list of the houses in Prozor that had been set on fire from the 23rd of October onwards. 1992 is the year concerned. If I have correctly noted your testimony, today you said that in April 1993 Ibrahim Sljivo's house was set on fire. Is that correct? Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Please have a look at the list and find the houses that were set on fire in April and tell us whether the house you mentioned is included in the list. So as not to waste time, this list doesn't include any houses burnt in April, and the name of Ibrahim Sljivo that you mentioned is not on the list either. Could you now have a look at the name Salko Konjaric. You said that his house was burned in June 1993. So as not to waste time, there is no information here about June, and this name that you've mentioned doesn't appear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Konjaric Hata. That's his mother. But the date is the 10th of May; perhaps I was a little mistaken when it comes to the date. Konjaric Hata. Under number 50.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So can I draw the conclusion that it was incorrect when you said that Salko Konjaric's house was set on fire in June? The answer is simple.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 10th of May. Well, I was a little mistaken when it comes to the date, but it's more or less that period. Konjaric Hata.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: We're talking about Salko Konjaric and about whether his house was set on fire in June. I have a few questions about this document. Can you tell us who compiled the document and when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I really don't know who compiled the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us when it was compiled? Approximately.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know, believe me.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: According to what you know, were some houses in Prozor damaged, set on fire, or destroyed as a result of the combat? Did any shells fall on houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: According to what you can see in the list, are those houses also included among the houses that were destroyed in Prozor from October 1992 onwards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Something was destroyed in the fighting, but most of them were torched.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, can you tell us whether in the Prozor municipality there was the Territorial Defence Staff headquarters?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to have to stop there. We've already gone on for an hour and a half. We have to make a 30-minute break now for technical reasons. Yes, the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I would like to ask the redaction of lines 67 -- page 67, line 11 to 19 as they might help in identifying the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's been done. We reconvene at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Counsel Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, may we just finish off discussing the document still on our screens. It is a list of facilities in Prozor municipality which were destroyed in one way or another from the 23rd of October onwards. Now, from what we've said so far -- or, rather, from what you've said so far about the document, we can conclude that this document contains the buildings and facilities destroyed in battle, during the fighting; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And we can conclude also that you cannot confirm who compiled this document and when; is that right? Witness, can you switch your microphone on, please, and could you repeat the answer to that last question of mine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, may the witness be shown P 00640, the next document. And I'd like to ask you to open the document in front of you. It is a list of confiscated vehicles -- or, rather, vehicles seized. Now, with respect to that document, you told us that on the list here there was the vehicle that was set fire to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, with all your education, are you able to conclude that the list is not a list of vehicles -- only vehicles seized or confiscated,, I assume you know what the term "confiscated" means.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So there are also vehicles on list which were not confiscated; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Most of them were confiscated, but there are vehicles, such as my brother's car, I know for sure was burnt.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, who and when was this list compiled? Who compiled the list and when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You told us that you worked in the municipality --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Counsel Alaburic, we gave you a lot of time, but you've already overstepped the time limit. You have taken up 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have been given time by the Praljak Defence, and I also consulted the Valentin Coric Defence, and they told me that they just need about 10 minutes. So can we ask the Prosecutor how much time they will need?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, they do not -- they do not have more than 10 minutes from the beginning, so there's nothing left over to give to you, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, they don't have anything to give me. All I'm saying is that they will need 10 minutes. So if the Prosecutor does not need additional time, I suggest that we use up today's session for listening to the witness, and if it's 10 minutes longer than what was provided for, I don't expect that will be a problem for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Get to the heart of the matter straight away then.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Madam Witness, I hope that this will still be important, because these are documents that we discussed that came from the Prosecution. You told us that you worked in the municipality up until the middle of 1993; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I take it that you weren't dismissed, nobody prevented you from working, and that you continued working just like you did before; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'd now like you to tell us if you compare the situation in 1993 to the situation that prevailed previously in the place you lived, would you agree with me when I say that there were a great many more people who came into your town from other places, Bugojno and other places like that from Central Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could these be counted in their thousands, thousands of new people coming into the Prozor area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me when I say that there were a great many members of military units as well in the Prozor municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm that in the Prozor area and the surrounding parts there were certain -- a certain amount of fighting going on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For what period are you asking?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The entire period, up until mid-1993. Until August 1993, let's say, when you left the town. Was there fighting going on, or was it just peaceful? I'm not asking you for the town itself, but I'm also asking you for the entire municipality and surrounding parts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was fighting.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that during that combat members of the civilian and military police were engaged as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm telling you that they were. Now, on that basis would it be logical to conclude that in view of the increased number of people in the town itself and the lack of policemen that it was very difficult to keep law and order, public law and order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can you repeat that question?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In view of the many more people who had come in to Prozor municipality and the fact that there were more military unit members and the general combat that was going on, the problems with food and many other problems that created a situation of chaos that it was very difficult to keep law and order or maintain public law and order in town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you also told us that to the best of your knowledge the civilian and military authorities on the territory of your municipality did nothing to establish public law and order linked to an order from General Milivoj Petkovic issued on the 31st of October.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'd just like to ask you something in that regard about several decisions, in fact, signed by the president of the civilian -- yes, if I can say so, the civilian HVO. And just a digression here: During 1993, did you work in a building in which Mr. Mijo Jozic was, too, where he had his office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to know that already in November 1992, a mixed Muslim-Croat commission was set up which was supposed to assess and determine the damage done to state and private facilities? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me what you know about that particular commission and what it established? Were people remunerated for the damage done?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The commission went round to visit the damaged facilities, torched facilities. They made a record, compiled a record and minutes of that, but people were never refunded for the damage done.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When you say "never," what period of time are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the time the damage was incurred to the present day.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can we then conclude that during the time that Prozor was not fully controlled by the HVO but by another power, people did -- received no remuneration for the damage that had been incurred to their property?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Well, the powers and authorities changed in Bosnia-Herzegovina. There were different people in power. So I'm asking you after the Washington agreements and Dayton Accords the powers that be established in Prozor, did they perhaps make up for the damages incurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. We'll deal with this subject later on through other witnesses. But do you happen to know a request made by Mr. Mijo Jozic to increase the number of policemen in the Prozor municipality so that law and order could be preserved? Do you know these efforts on his part, that is to say to increase the number of policemen on the police force?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you know an order issued by the chief of the military police to have vehicles returned who -- which were confiscated contrary to legal provisions in Prozor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you know about the conclusion made by the municipal authorities of your town to replace and dismiss all those who took part in any looting and who engaged in crimes on the territory of Prozor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you now tell me, in view of your education, these decisions that I picked, had you known about these decisions would you still claim that the HVO authorities did nothing to preserve law and order or establish law and order in Prozor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You would stand by your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Regardless of these decisions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you explain how that is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the situation in the field was --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about the results. I'm asking you about the efforts made to do something. I assume you can differentiate between the endeavours on the part of the authorities to do something and the results of their efforts. So I'm just asking you about their efforts, the steps they undertook and efforts they made. We'll leave the results of that alone and discuss them in due course. But all the conclusions and decisions that I mentioned a moment ago, which I just selected at random by way of example, can confirm that the authorities did indeed wish to establish public law and order.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the basis of documents the answer would be yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Just one more question with the Court's indulgence, and it is linked to your statement. You told us -- or, actually, you didn't tell us but it was recorded in your statement, the statement of the 6th of February, 2002, that after the conflict in October 1992, most of the men decided not to remain in Prozor and that they left and went to Jablanica or Gornji Vakuf. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The people's whose houses had been devastated went to Jablanica and Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let me remind you, with the Court's indulgence, of a portion of your statement of the 6th of February, 2002, and it is contained on page 6 of the English version and page 8 of the -- or 6 of the Croatian version and 5 of the English version. You didn't speak about the departure of men who lived in the houses which had been destroyed, but you refer to men who -- or males who for security reasons went to Jablanica and Gornji Vakuf and joined up with the BH army forces there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, they were mostly people who didn't have anywhere to go. They couldn't return to their own houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So the males didn't have any place to return went to Jablanica and Gornji Vakuf, and those males without a roof over their heads left their women, children, and elderly people. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Whole families left.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I see, whole families left. Now, on those same pages of that statement of yours, you said that the women, children, and elderly persons remained in Prozor while the men, for the most part, left to Jablanica and Gornji Vakuf to join up with the BH army forces there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. But I should have added those who didn't have anywhere to live in Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So the men who didn't have anywhere to live left.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They left with their families.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Right. They left with their families. That means that in 2002, when you gave this statement, you did not tell us the exact -- describe the exact situation. Now, two more questions. You mentioned in your statements that the men left, the women stayed, and that the women asked the president of the municipality to organise a convoy in order to leave town; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not those women. Not the women that left.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Well, no, not the women who left, of course, the women who stayed on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but they didn't ask those men, but the women who were in town with their own families.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So the women who were in town with their husbands asked that a convoy to leave town be organised.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to us how the women went to ask for this and not the men, not their husbands who lived in the same town, or at least a mixed delegation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All I know is that the women came to talk to the president for the population to be evacuated because the living conditions were terrible.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us this: You and most other witnesses who left the Prozor municipality told us that they left and went to Bugojno. Can you tell us whether you received any instructions, particular instructions to go to Bugojno, or how come you decided to go precisely to Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We didn't have anywhere else to go.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So it was only the road leading to Bugojno that was free, there was free passage on that road. You couldn't take any other route?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: How come some people went to Jablanica and Vakuf then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Jablanica Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They didn't go then. They had left previously.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: How did some people from Jablanica go towards Bugojno as well, even going on foot for a great part -- for a lot of the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know about that. Perhaps that happened, but I really don't know. All I do know is that the population mostly moved to Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were concentrated in Bugojno. Now, I'm interested in knowing how they happened to go precisely to Bugojno and stay there. Can you explain that to us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they didn't have anywhere else to go.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And how did you learn about the fact that there was an area in Bugojno where you could be accommodated? Did anyone tell you that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Madam, nobody told us that, but since we spent a little time in Celina, in Buturovic Polje, they told us there were room in Bugojno, so most of the population went to Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Who told you that there was some room in Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one more question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
